paras: The killing of Ike Kinney took place on August 3, 1905, when a posse of citizens shot Kinney, a Black man, dead in a river bottom at Doella, a plantation post office six miles south of Lewisville, Arkansas. Kinney had been hunted for about a day after he was accused of killing a Black man at Stamps and then shooting E. R. Ferguson, a railroad claim agent riding with a posse. A wire special from Lewisville listing his 'bloody record' of two killings and four woundings ran in dozens of papers, including the Black weekly St. Louis Palladium.

According to a dispatch from Stamps dated August 2, Kinney killed a Black man at Stamps that morning and escaped. Posses went after him, and about three miles from town one of them met him in the woods, where he opened fire and killed Ferguson, claim agent of the Louisiana and Arkansas railroad. Kinney escaped again, the Bodcaw Lumber Company offered $500 for his capture, and special trains went to Pine Bluff and to Minden, Louisiana, for bloodhounds. The Pine Bluff Daily Graphic, writing before his death was known, reported that excitement was running high and that he would likely be lynched if found.

At 3 a.m. on August 3, three miles from Lewisville, Kinney was said to have fired four shots from a Winchester into a couple named Stewart from Greensburg, wounding Mrs. Stewart in the breast and her husband in the side. The same report has him telling the couple that he had taken them for members of a posse and was sorry he had fired. That morning about twenty-five men with dogs took up his trail after a man on a river farm reported that a Black man had asked him for water and to be taken across the Red River.

Searchers located Kinney in a bottom near Doella, and a posse left Lewisville shortly before noon on a special train. As it closed in, by the posse's account, Kinney opened fire, taking a finger off C. F. Nash and shooting Alvin Barham through the neck, before W. C. Nash shot him dead. By then $1,500 had been offered for him 'dead or alive.'
The posse brought Kinney's body back to Stamps on the special train. No report of an inquest, and no name for the man killed at Stamps, appears in the coverage.

Nearly every later account derived from one special from Lewisville to the Gazette at Little Rock, which the Associated Press sent out on August 3. White headlines and rewrites cast Kinney as a 'Bad Negro' with a 'Bloody Record', a 'desperate and murderous negro' and, in the Richmond Times Dispatch, a 'Wild Man Chased Into River Bottom'. The Arizona Republican instead headlined his apology to the Stewarts as a 'Negro Misapprehension'. Rewrites spread errors, moving the scene to 'Lewisville, Kan.', 'Doella, Kan.' or 'Joella', and renaming him Isaac or Guy Kinney.

In the Black press the story appeared only in the St. Louis Palladium of August 5, in a short form of the Gazette special. Its headline, 'If Reports of His Doings Are Correct He Was Not Suppressed Any Too Soon,' and the column around it were identical to those in the white Lexington Advertiser of Mississippi, showing that the Palladium ran syndicated copy rather than its own comment. No Black paper questioned the posse's account or reported the killing in its own words.

An early Stamps special called the claim agent 'E. W. Ferguson, general agent of the Texas & Arkansas railroad' and the killer 'Guy Kinney', against the 'E. R. Ferguson' of the Louisiana and Arkansas and 'Ike Kinney' given by the Pine Bluff paper and the Gazette special. All versions of the fights at Stamps and Doella come from the pursuers, and none gives Kinney's own account or a reason for the first killing.

reader.title: Killing of Ike Kinney
bases: Ike Kinney, a Black man accused of two killings, was shot dead by a posse of citizens that had surrounded him in a river bottom after he fired on it (A5, A6, A1).

A posse of citizens (about twenty-five men set out, joined by a posse sent by special train) shot Kinney dead while he was at large and, by its own account, firing on it, so the reports describe a killing in an armed pursuit rather than the killing of a captive; no officer or legal warrant is named, and a lynching was only predicted before his death (A5, A6, A4).

The early Stamps reports (A1, A3, A4) and the later Gazette special from Lewisville (A5, A6) agree on the core events, though every account comes from the pursuers' side and the Gazette special was the source of nearly all later versions.

accounts.label: Gazette special from Lewisville (posse's account)
accounts.gist: After shooting the Stewarts, Kinney was tracked to a river bottom near Doella, where he fired on the closing posse, wounding two, and W. C. Nash shot him dead.

framing.detail: Headlines framed Kinney as a 'Bad Negro' with a 'Bloody Record', a 'Negro Desperado' and a 'Wild Man Chased Into River Bottom'.
The Pine Bluff Daily Graphic, before his death was known, reported calmly that he would likely be lynched if found and praised Ferguson as a prominent citizen.

The St. Louis Palladium carried the same syndicated column as a Mississippi white weekly, headed 'If Reports of His Doings Are Correct He Was Not Suppressed Any Too Soon', with only a conditional hedge.
